summary:
Burundi criminalises same-sex conduct. The prohibition dates from the 2009 penal code, and US State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gays and lesbians under that framework, together with arrests and harassment of LGBT people. No source in this inventory identifies any protection, exemption or decriminalisation measure.

The risk posture escalated in December 2023, when President Évariste Ndayishimiye publicly called for homosexuals to be "stoned", adding "that's what they deserve". Human Rights Watch, reporting in January 2024, condemned the remarks as stoking fear among LGBT people and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, the Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation operating in exile, characterised the speech as "a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people".

Burundians living under the criminalisation regime reported terror in the weeks that followed. SOS Médias Burundi, writing in January 2024, quoted members of two LGBTQ associations speaking anonymously, who described the presidential remarks as "a real license to kill (us)". The same reporting restates that same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2015 report on Burundi places the section on violence and discrimination against LGBT persons within a broader account of the country's crisis, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns. The 2010 report lists discrimination against gays and lesbians alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions, while the 2012 report documents torture, extrajudicial executions and prolonged pretrial detention. Enforcement of the sodomy law therefore sits within a security apparatus already recorded as using lethal and arbitrary force.

The principal organised Burundian LGBTQ rights voice, the Iteka League, operates from exile rather than inside the country, which shapes how protection and reporting reach Burundian communities.

Discrimination against gays and lesbians has been recorded continuously across US State Department reporting for 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015, with arrests and harassment documented under the 2009 penal code.

Following the December 2023 speech, LGBTQ Burundians described themselves as living in fear. Two association members, quoted anonymously by SOS Médias Burundi in January 2024, said the remarks amounted to a licence to kill them. The Iteka League, in exile, urged recognition of the speech as a call for lynching, while Human Rights Watch called on the ruling party to renounce persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, visa or entry screening that could disclose a person's status, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, same-sex partnership or marriage recognition, restroom or facility access rules, or restrictions on gender-affirming care. Whether any of these exist, and in what form, remains unresolved on the available material.

The inventory does not state the specific article or penalty range of the 2009 penal code provision criminalising same-sex conduct, nor does it record a prosecution, conviction or acquittal under that provision with a date and outcome. It also does not establish whether the presidential remarks of December 2023 were followed by any formal enforcement directive or arrests.
